title: Reading the world clock: three rows, DST and IANA zones
description: Site world clock: each card has a UTC time row, a local date row and an offset badge versus your browser, plus DST, half-hour rounding and IANA traps.
content:
The site's world clock shows several time zones side by side. Every card has three rows: a time row, a date row and an offset badge. The three rows follow different conventions, and almost every misreading starts there.

Three rows per card: UTC time, local date, offset versus local

The page ships 14 time zones: Beijing (time zone Asia/Shanghai), Tokyo, London and New York are shown by default, the dropdown holds the other 10, and an option reads like "Hong Kong (Asia/Hong_Kong)". City names come from a hard-coded table, and with all 14 cards added every one matched its name.

The time row comes from an Intl.DateTimeFormat with a hard-coded timeZone: 'UTC', so it never follows the city. Frozen at 2026-01-15T03:00:00Z, all four cards show 03:00:00 in the time row; at that instant Shanghai local time is 11:00:00, Tokyo 12:00:00, London 03:00:00 and New York 22:00:00 on 14 January.

The date row takes year, month and day from each zone's own calendar, in the format yyyy/mm/dd (for example 2026/01/15): at the same instant Shanghai, Tokyo and London all read 2026/01/15, while New York already reads 2026/01/14. The badge is a third convention again: it compares the zone's offset with the browser's own, showing "same as local" for 0, "+8h vs local" for a positive difference and "-5h vs local" for a negative one.

CityTime rowDate rowBadge (UTC browser)Local actual time
Beijing03:00:002026/01/15+8h vs local11:00:00
Tokyo03:00:002026/01/15+9h vs local12:00:00
London03:00:002026/01/15same as local03:00:00
New York03:00:002026/01/14-5h vs local22:00:00 (14 January)

Read the three rows together and the contradiction is plain: the New York card shows 03:00:00 in the time row and 2026/01/14 in the date row, yet it is 22:00 there at that moment. The time row is not wrong; it is simply UTC. In the screenshot the time row reads 03:00:01, a second past the 03:00:00 in the table — the page repaints every second, so the capture froze on the frame after the tick.

The offset badge measures the gap to your own machine

offsetOf(tz) reads the zone's wall-clock time on every render, treats it as UTC, subtracts the current instant and rounds to whole hours; then -new Date().getTimezoneOffset()/60 gives the local offset, and subtracting that from the zone offset yields diff. With a UTC browser the local offset is 0, so the badge happens to equal the absolute offset: Shanghai +8, Tokyo +9, London 0, New York -5. This is exactly where over-generalizing starts.

In a browser context with timezoneId: 'Asia/Shanghai', the time row is still 03:00:00 (UTC) and the date row is still 01/15 for Shanghai and 01/14 for New York, but the four badges become "same as local", "+1h vs local", "-8h vs local" and "-13h vs local". Same code, same instant; only the browser time zone changed.

So "-5h vs local" equals New York's UTC offset only in a UTC browser, and the browser time zone is not necessarily UTC (this run's screenshot and test environment happened to be UTC). The midnight case exposes the mixed conventions best: at 2026-11-10T00:00:00Z the New York card shows 00:00:00 / 2026/11/09 / -5h vs local, while it is 19:00:00 in New York.

Format detail: hour12: false together with hour: '2-digit' follows h23 under zh-CN, so midnight prints 00 rather than 24, and all four cards in this run showed 00:00:00.

Daylight saving time: the offset moves, and a day is not always 24 hours

The badge is not a constant. offsetOf runs again on every render, so the badge can change with the date. Around New York's two switch points, sampling one point on each side (30 seconds before and 30 seconds after): 2026-03-08T06:59:30Z is -5, 07:00:30Z is -4; 2026-11-01T05:59:30Z is -4, 06:00:30Z is -5 again. London is clearer still: "same as local" on 15 January, "+1h vs local" on 15 July.

The switch also creates local times that do not exist, or that exist twice. Scanning New York local time minute by minute through 2026-03-08, the 300 minutes contain no 02:xx: 01:59 is followed straight by 03:00, and at the switch the card's time row is 07:00:30 while it is already 03:00:30 locally.

The other direction overlaps instead: on 2026-11-01 New York's 01:00 happens twice, once at 05:00:00Z and once at 06:00:00Z, so the whole 01:xx hour holds 60 repeated local times. For an appointment inside that hour, "New York 01:30" is not enough.

The southern hemisphere runs the other way: Sydney is +660 minutes in January and +600 in July, so with a UTC browser the badge reads +11h vs local in January and +10h vs local in July. China used daylight saving time too: Asia/Shanghai is +540 minutes on 1988-07-15 and +480 on 1988-01-15; on 1991-07-15 it is still +540, and by 1992-07-15 it is back at +480. So "China has no daylight saving time" was not always true: in these samples the summers of 1988 and 1991 are both +540, and only the summer of 1992 is back at +480.

All 14 built-in zones are whole hours, so half-hour zones get rounded

All 14 built-in zones are a whole multiple of 60 minutes at both sample instants (2026-01-15T03:00:00Z and 2026-07-15T03:00:00Z). In the January sample Dubai is +240, Moscow +180, Sao Paulo -180 and Auckland +780; not one is a half hour.

Half-hour and 45-minute zones do exist in IANA, though, and ICU gives these offsets in minutes for fixed instants:

  • Asia/Kolkata: +330 minutes (UTC+5:30), the same at both sample instants.
  • Asia/Kathmandu: +345 minutes (UTC+5:45).
  • Australia/Adelaide: +630 minutes in January and +570 in July; the half-hour offset also follows daylight saving time.
  • Pacific/Chatham: +825 minutes in January and +765 in July (UTC+13:45 / +12:45).

Feed them into the page formula Math.round((asUtc - now) / 3600000): Kolkata's +5:30 becomes +6, 30 minutes too many; Kathmandu's +5:45 also becomes +6, 15 minutes too many; Adelaide's +9:30 in July becomes +10; Chatham's +13:45 in January becomes +14. The negative side is just as uneven: America/St_Johns at -3:30 becomes -3, 30 minutes short.

These are inferences from the page formula plus ICU data, not interface measurements: the dropdown holds only the 14 whole-hour zones and there is no field for an arbitrary zone name. They show that the formula keeps whole hours only, which costs nothing on the built-in list and produces an error outside it.

IANA names: not a city list, and a sign trap

Zone names come from the IANA tz database in an "Area/Location" form, such as Asia/Shanghai and America/New_York. The database is updated regularly, and browsers and Node each carry their own ICU data, so one name can yield different historical or future rules across versions.

The names are not a city list. IANA's naming notes explicitly prefer Asia/Shanghai over Asia/Beijing; handing Asia/Beijing to Intl.DateTimeFormat throws RangeError: Invalid time zone specified: Asia/Beijing, and an empty string, Not/AZone and Asia/Shanghai/Extra are rejected just the same.

Aliases are another layer: Asia/Calcutta and Asia/Kolkata are the same zone, formatting identically and both at +330 minutes; in this ICU the canonical name is in fact the older Asia/Calcutta, and resolvedOptions().timeZone maps Kolkata back to Calcutta.

Abbreviations are not reliable zone names: in this run's Node 22 ICU, CST raises no error and is parsed as America/Chicago (-360 minutes in winter); IANA also warns that CST means different things in China and North America and recommends a numeric offset instead.

Offset identifiers are a second kind of valid input: +08:00 raises no error and 03:00Z renders as 11:00. ECMA-402 defines the time-zone internal slot as either a named time zone identifier or an offset time zone identifier. Watch the legacy names: Etc/GMT-8 is really +480 minutes (UTC+8) and Etc/GMT+8 is -480 (UTC-8), the sign running opposite to the direction; Etc/UTC is 0.

Sign convention: getTimezoneOffset() returns how many minutes local time is behind UTC, so UTC+8 gives -480 and UTC-5 gives 300; the page's -new Date().getTimezoneOffset()/60 flips it back. MDN's example is the same, with UTC+10 returning -600.

The supported list is not every usable name either: Intl.supportedValuesOf('timeZone') returned 418 entries in this run, including Asia/Shanghai and Asia/Calcutta, but not the alias Asia/Kolkata and not UTC.

How to use this tool correctly

Treat the three rows as three different things: the time row is UTC, the date row is the local calendar, the badge is the gap to your own machine. To answer "what time is it in London", you cannot simply add the time row and the badge: the badge is the gap to your own machine, and it equals the absolute offset only when your own time zone happens to be UTC. The safe approach is to set the browser or the browser context to UTC, so the badge equals the UTC offset, or to move the same instant into the target zone with the Timestamp Converter.

  • Check the date row across midnight: at one instant Shanghai reads 2026/01/15 and New York 2026/01/14, and the time row alone suggests the same day on both sides.
  • Do not read the badge as an absolute offset: for that, set the browser or the browser context to UTC, and only then does the badge match the UTC offset.
  • Do not read "same as local" as "same as UTC": under a UTC browser London matches only in winter, and in July the badge becomes "+1h vs local".
  • When you agree a time across zones, write the zone name and the date: inside the repeated hour "New York 01:30" can mean two instants, and the Date Difference Calculator helps check the day count.

Interface details: 4 cards by default and 10 options in the dropdown; adding one takes the cards to +1 and the options to -1, and the new card's time row matches the first card's. With all 14 added the dropdown is empty, and pressing "Add" again raises "Time zone already added". The remove button sits in the top right corner: removing a card drops the count by 1 and puts the zone back in the dropdown; remove them all and you get 0 cards with no empty-state text in the grid, which looks broken but is just an empty list. A refresh returns to the default 4, because the selection is not saved.

The page repaints the whole block every second: render() replaces grid.innerHTML wholesale and a setInterval(render, 1000) is attached. Pause at 03:00:00 and let one second tick: all four old card nodes leave the document and the time row becomes 03:00:01; one more second and the previous nodes are replaced again. Scrapers have to re-query the nodes every time.

No cross-origin requests go out: in this run the whole round was same-origin (247 GETs), with 0 POSTs.

Boundaries and limits

The time row is always UTC; the date row is the local calendar; the badge is a whole-hour gap to the browser. The page never says that the three rows differ, and there is no switch to "show local time".

The badge is accurate only to the hour and only on whole-hour zones. A daylight saving switch moves it by an hour; half-hour or 45-minute zones put through the same formula are rounded, an error of 15 to 30 minutes; changing device or system time zone changes the badge too.

Only 14 zones are available, hard-coded in an array, with no search or custom input; the selection is not persisted; deleting everything leaves no empty state and no hint about the minimum or maximum count.

The data comes from the runtime's ICU/tzdata, and this run's Node 22.23.4 carries ICU 78.3. Historical offsets and future rules change with the version; IANA 2026f is already out, and browsers and Node update on different schedules, so when a government changes a rule local computation can only follow the data it has.

This article only describes what this page did across the 68 browser cases and 34 Node/ICU checks run for it. It is not advice on cross-time-zone meetings, travel or billing, and it does not validate whether an entered time makes sense.

faqs.q: Why do all four cards show the same time row?
faqs.a: The time row uses an Intl.DateTimeFormat with a hard-coded timeZone: "UTC" that every card shares, so it only shows the current UTC instant. What changes is the date row (each zone's own calendar) and the offset badge (relative to the browser's own time zone).

faqs.q: Why does the New York card show 00:00:00 on the previous day's date?
faqs.a: The time row is UTC and the date row is New York's own calendar. At 2026-11-10T00:00:00Z it is 19:00 on 9 November in New York, so the card shows 00:00:00 in the time row, 2026/11/09 in the date row and "-5h vs local" in the badge (with a UTC browser). The three rows are not one convention.

faqs.q: Is "-5h vs local" New York's UTC offset?
faqs.a: No, it is the gap between New York and the browser's own machine. Under a UTC browser the gap happens to be -5 hours; switch to a browser context set to Asia/Shanghai and the same card becomes "-13h vs local", while New York's absolute offset is still UTC-5.

faqs.q: Why can't I add Kolkata or Kathmandu?
faqs.a: The page has only the 14 hard-coded zones and no entry for an arbitrary zone name, so neither city is in the dropdown at all. Even feeding a similar zone into the page formula, offsetOf's Math.round keeps whole hours only: +5:30 is computed as +6, and +5:45 as +6 too.

sources.title: Theory and pragmatics of the tz code and data

focus: The world clock card's time row is hard-coded to UTC, the date row follows each zone's own calendar, and the offset badge is a whole-hour gap to the browser; when the target zone's daylight saving switches are out of step with the browser time zone's, the badge jumps by an hour at the switch, and switch days produce local times that do not exist or repeat; all 14 built-in zones are whole hours, and the page's Math.round formula rounds half-hour zones; IANA names bring aliases, abbreviations and the Etc/GMT sign trap, and an invalid name throws a RangeError.
